body: Sunday, October 11 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed is in an active tightening bias. FOMC minutes released this past week showed unanimous support for the September rate hike, with officials signaling another hike is likely but offering no firm guidance on timing. The 10Y yield has surged to 5.24% (+27 bps vs 4 weeks ago) and the 2Y sits at 4.80% (prior close, +17 bps vs 4W), producing a +44 bps curve (prior close) that is positive but still flat by historical standards — a structurally unusual combination of rising long rates alongside equity strength. Fiscal dominance is the defining feature: the Treasury term premium continues to expand as deficits remain unaddressed under Trump's second term.

New / Most Important: The most consequential signal this week is the growing debate among economists over whether the Fed will hike again this year, with ABC News reporting divided views. A top Fed official cast doubt on a move this month, suggesting a skip-then-hike pattern. Big bank earnings begin this coming week and will be the first real-time read on how 5%+ long rates are filtering through net interest margins, loan demand, and credit quality. The S&P 500 at 7811 (↑2.0%) hovering near all-time highs while the Russell 2000 at 2807 (↓3.3%) diverges sharply tells you this is a liquidity-concentration trade, not a broad expansion — Russell/Nasdaq ratio down 8.1% in 4 weeks is extreme mega-cap dominance.

Playbook ✓: Mega-cap AI beneficiaries carrying the index while rate-sensitive small-caps and real estate lag — textbook narrow-market-in-a-tightening-cycle behavior. VIX at 14.84 in complacency territory is consistent with the "bad news is ignored until it isn't" phase.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The structural anomaly is equities making all-time highs with the 10Y at 5.24%. This breaks every traditional playbook. The explanation is capital flow mechanics: foreign capital rotating out of European and EM duration into US mega-cap equity as a quasi-fixed-income substitute (high free-cash-flow yields on AAPL/MSFT/NVDA rival or exceed sovereign yields in many jurisdictions). The 30-year mortgage rate at 7.40%, its highest in nearly three years, alongside the equity strength signals this is not a genuine risk-on environment — it's a bifurcated market where rate-sensitive housing is cracking while mega-cap equity is bought. ISM manufacturing easing to 54.5 while its prices index jumped to 77.9 points to supply-shock rather than demand-pull dynamics, which could complicate the Fed's inflation calculus if energy re-accelerates. Watch bank earnings this week for evidence that 5%+ yields are starting to crack commercial real estate and consumer credit — if delinquencies are climbing while NIMs are expanding, the market will have to price a profits-recession-with-tight-policy scenario that equities haven't discounted.

Macro Stance: The ECB is navigating a painful bind — inflation upside risks persist (confirmed by ECB accounts this week) while growth deterioration argues for a pause. The consensus as of this week is that the ECB will pause in October before potentially hiking again in December. French fiscal stress is a dominant theme, with Politico and DWS both drawing explicit parallels to euro-crisis dynamics.

New / Most Important: French fiscal risks have materially escalated and are now cited as a reason the ECB may pause after December — this represents a new constraint on ECB policy where sovereign stress in a core member state is actively shaping rate decisions. The EU trade chief headed to China this past week as Brussels prepares trade actions, setting up a potential two-front economic war (fiscal fragility + trade escalation). The ECB's push for wide digital euro adoption from first issuance signals they view CBDC as a strategic sovereignty tool, not just a payments upgrade.

Playbook ✓: Dollar bulls pressing on European weakness, European auto stocks having a terrible year, and the ECB hiking into weakness — all consensus. Morningstar flagged turbulent earnings season ahead for European equities.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: France's debt troubles are no longer a peripheral concern — they are actively constraining ECB monetary policy for the entire eurozone. This is structurally new. In previous cycles, the ECB's rate path was set primarily by aggregate inflation; now a single sovereign's fiscal trajectory is creating a binding constraint. If French spreads widen enough to force the ECB to pause or cut before inflation is controlled, it would represent the first time since Draghi's "whatever it takes" that fiscal dominance overrode the ECB's inflation mandate. The transmission to global assets runs through EUR weakness (boosting DXY), European bank equity stress, and potentially a flight from European duration into US assets — reinforcing the dollar-centric capital flow loop.

Macro Stance: The easing bias runs through liquidity and the balance sheet, not the policy rate. The PBOC is conducting a 1.2 trillion yuan outright reverse repo (巴士的報, [Oct 8]) and bought a net 100 billion yuan of sovereign bonds in September (TradingView, [Oct 9]), so China's bond yields are falling as they surge everywhere else (Quartz, [Oct 8]); with US 10Y yields at 5.24%, the rate gap keeps a benchmark cut off the table. The currency is not the pressure point the dollar rally implies: the central bank says it has no need or intention to weaken the yuan for a trade edge (The Standard (HK), [Oct 8]), the yuan hit a four-year high against its basket (Bloomberg, [Oct 8]) and the fix firmed to 6.7330 from 6.7367 (www.tmgm.com, [Oct 9]). Prices no longer bind: August CPI rose 0.8% and PPI 3.8% (BigGo Finance, [Sep 8]), and September CPI is on this week's calendar (Newsquawk, [Oct 9]).

PMIs & Activity: September's official manufacturing PMI returned to growth at 50.1, exactly at consensus and up from 49.8, with non-manufacturing at 50.2 (investingLive, [Sep 29]); the private RatingDog gauges were stronger at 52.1 and 51.6 (investingLive, [Sep 30]), and Reuters ties the factory expansion to the AI boom (Reuters, [Sep 29]). The domestic half lags: August retail sales rose 0.4% against 0.6% expected (investingLive, [Sep 14]) and industrial profit growth slowed to 4.2% (Bloomberg, [Sep 27]). The holiday did not change that split: Golden Week spending per trip hit a four-year low (Gulf Times, [Oct 10]) and September passenger-vehicle retail sales dropped 24% (Bloomberg, [Oct 10]). Nikkei estimates third-quarter growth at 4.4%, below target (Nikkei Asia, [Oct 6]).

Credit Impulse: The last print is August's, weak on both measures: bank lending disappointed as credit demand stayed weak (Reuters, [Sep 14]) and total credit expansion missed forecasts (Bloomberg, [Sep 14]), with bond and equity financing exceeding loans in social financing for the first time (BigGo Finance, [Sep 14]); the government-bond leg held up while private loan demand did not. The state subsidises credit rather than igniting it: the finance ministry says 100 billion yuan of interest subsidies leveraged 17 trillion yuan of consumer credit (BigGo Finance, [Oct 9]). Meanwhile China is consolidating nearly one in four banks as strains hit smaller lenders (NTD News, [Oct 5]).

Property: Golden Week gave the clearest demand signal in months. New-home subscriptions in 50 key cities rose over 15% year on year (Moomoo, [Oct 8]), Shanghai new-home sales doubled and second-hand transactions in 11 cities jumped over 40% (BigGo Finance, [Oct 9]), and the mortgage subsidy is credited with lifting holiday homebuying (iChongqing, [Oct 10]); Bloomberg still calls it a modest recovery (Bloomberg, [Oct 8]). Top-100 developers sold 242 billion yuan in September (www.grihik.com, [Oct 8]). Balance sheets remain the weak point: Vanke reported a 16.02 billion yuan loss (ad-hoc-news.de, [Oct 7]) and PAG is in exclusive talks for a stake in an Evergrande unit (Reuters, [Oct 8]). The base is August's: prices down across 70 cities and investment down 19.9% in eight months (BigGo Finance, [Sep 14]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Beijing lets local governments tap 550 billion yuan of unused debt quotas (Caixin Global, [Oct 9]), a fiscal push to meet the growth target (Reuters, [Oct 9]), and the NDRC pledges more policy tools (Bloomberg, [Oct 10]); but the growing debt burden limits space for stimulus (Financial Times, [Oct 10]) and the WSJ calls it half measures (WSJ, [Oct 8]). On trade, the EU and China struck a deal to halve Chinese hybrid exports (Reuters, [Oct 9]) within a 16-point consensus that covers export controls (Global Times, [Oct 9]). Britain is the next front, with Beijing warning of serious concern over its EV tariff plan (The Telegraph, [Oct 6]), and the US rare-earth truce was extended by just two months (Startup Fortune, [Oct 7]). The export engine behind it surged 25% in August (Nikkei Asia, [Sep 8]).

Markets & Flows: China stocks hit an over one-year low as the AI selloff deepened (The Economic Times, [Oct 9]) and the Hang Seng fell to a three-month low on the first day back (The Standard (HK), [Oct 8]) before a 1.79% rebound (Moomoo, [Oct 9]) on unconfirmed talk of regulator guidance (Bloomberg, [Oct 9]). Breakingviews argues China's slow bull market is poised to take off (Reuters, [Oct 8]), while Yahoo Finance asks why China is missing the AI rally (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 9]).

New / Most Important: The Golden Week verdict is split. Housing responded to the subsidy, with Shanghai new-home sales doubling, while spending per trip hit a four-year low and car sales fell 24%; Beijing's answer is 550 billion yuan of quota and more NDRC tools rather than a rate cut. The EU hybrid deal removes the near-term tariff tail but caps the export channel that carried August.

Playbook ✓: Property in controlled deflation with a subsidy-driven bounce, incremental quota releases, liquidity through outright repos and bond buying, and exports diverting around tariffs are all consensus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The structural divergence is China's absence from the global AI equity trade even as AI drives its factory PMI. If the slow-bull thesis gains traction, the re-rating catalyst will be AI re-pricing, not consumption, pulling capital from US mega-cap tech and supporting the yuan. Transmission elsewhere stays narrow: an AI-led PMI helps Asian tech supply chains; the housing bounce is the first to reach the demand iron ore and the AUD need, but with property investment down 19.9% and credit missing, the AUD, whose own factory PMI fell to 49.6 on falling new orders (investingLive, [Sep 30]), gets sentiment rather than an impulse. European autos gain from a cap on Chinese hybrids, but luxury needs a consumer whose spending per trip just hit a four-year low.

Macro Stance: The BoJ remains in a pussyfooting normalization — QT is being used to support the yen while rate hikes are being delayed and re-delayed. A dovish dissenter signaled support for future hikes, suggesting internal consensus is building, but markets have scaled back near-term hike expectations. The yen weakened to the lower 158 range against the dollar this past week.

New / Most Important: The Chosun Ilbo reported the BoJ is weighing a second rate hike specifically as the yen carry trade unwinds — this frames the next hike as a financial stability decision rather than an inflation decision, which changes the reaction function entirely. Wolf Street highlighted the BoJ is accelerating QT to prop up the yen, effectively using balance sheet policy as a substitute for rate policy. A reflationist ex-BoJ policymaker called an end to the era of low rates and big spending, which represents a notable shift in the intellectual ecosystem around the BoJ.

Playbook ✓: Yen weakness, carry trade persistence, and BoJ communication ambiguity are all consensus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The divergence is the BoJ using QT as a yen management tool while delaying rate hikes — effectively decoupling its two policy instruments in opposite directions. This is unusual and creates fragility: if the yen breaks meaningfully below 160, the BoJ may be forced into an emergency hike that disrupts global carry positions. With US 10Y at 5.24%, the US-Japan rate differential is enormous, making the yen carry trade enormously attractive and the eventual unwind enormously disruptive.

Macro Stance: The RBA remains in a tightening posture after a recent rate rise that caught some off guard. Consumer confidence plunged to its worst level since the 1990s following the hike, per Guardian and AFR reports this week. Mortgage burden has reached levels last seen in 1989. The RBA has been explicitly criticized for being caught off guard by inflation.

New / Most Important: The consumer confidence collapse to 30-year lows is a material new data point — this is the kind of demand destruction that typically precedes a hard-landing dynamic. Manufacturers accused the RBA of undermining productivity, signaling that the political economy constraint on further tightening is intensifying. The AUD declined as RBA hike bets faded and US yields climbed.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The AFR simultaneously ran a piece arguing high rates "aren't hurting households like they used to" — contradicting the confidence data. This disconnect suggests the transmission mechanism is bifurcated: asset-rich homeowners are cushioned by home equity and savings buffers, while renters and recent buyers are being crushed. This two-speed economy makes the RBA's job nearly impossible — aggregate data looks resilient while the marginal consumer is in crisis. AUD is a China-beta play; if China re-rates positively (per Reuters' slow-bull thesis), AUD could rally despite domestic macro weakness.

Macro Stance: Sunday brings no new data, so the stance rests on the week's three facts: the RPP held at 3.75% (Strefa Inwestorów [Oct 7]); Glapiński does not foresee a November hike but says the Council is ready to act (PAP Biznes [Oct 8]); and the November projection is the trigger (Forex Club [Oct 7]). The hawkish tail is real. September inflation came in above the reference rate itself (Polskie Radio 24 [Oct 7]), Business Insider Polska [Oct 9] reports the RPP warning about 2027 as fuel and commodity prices climb, and ING expects hikes to arrive in 2027 with inflation able to exceed 3.5% (CEO Magazyn [Oct 8]). Against that, Strefa Biznesu [Oct 8] reads the governor as calming, and Newsmax [Oct 8] notes fuel is not feeding core prices. The growth side keeps improving: GUS raised 2025 GDP to 3.8% (wnp.pl [Oct 6]), xyz.pl [Oct 11] says the economy holds strong against a difficult backdrop even as its growth record is put to the test, and Domański reports more institutions raising forecasts (pb.pl [Oct 6]). Wages are the soft spot: the April median of 7695 zł, about 20% below the average (Business Insider Polska [Oct 7]) and a one-year low in economic sentiment (CEO Magazyn [Oct 7]).

Markets: The week closed with Warsaw up and rotation into energy and consumer names (Parkiet, Inwestycje.pl [Oct 9]). On the card, Orlen at 159.34 is up 10.4% on the week, PGE at 16.7 up 11.1% and 19.0% over four weeks, Dino at 35.81 up 6.4%, LPP at 25040 up 4.2% and 16.1% over four weeks, CD Projekt at 263.0 up 3.7% and 11.7% over four weeks, KGHM at 347.0 up 3.5%, Allegro at 51.75 up 2.7%. Banks are the drag: PKO at 113.94 is down 3.6% on the week and 5.5% over four weeks, Pekao at 261.1 down 2.8%. EPOL closed 43.82, up 1.8% on the week and down 3.8% over four weeks. USD/PLN closed 3.9015, up 0.3% on the week and 4.8% over four weeks; EUR/PLN closed 4.3752, flat on the week and up 1.2% over four weeks. The forecast community is turning: BGK economists now project EUR/PLN falling toward 4.3 (FXMAG [Oct 11]), and the dollar ended the week back under 3.90 (Comparic [Oct 9]) after its Oct 8 high. On rates, a ZBP and SGH report warns bank holdings of government debt may crowd out company lending (Portal Samorządowy [Oct 9]), and wGospodarce [Oct 11] puts it bluntly: state debt is blocking Polish banks. Parkiet [Oct 9] identifies new engines that could pull WIG20 higher.

Fiscal & Politics: The 2027 budget, with its 281.2bn zł deficit and almost 200bn zł for defence (Portal Samorządowy [Oct 8]), is in Sejm committee (Super Biznes [Oct 9]). Weekend coverage is about who pays: Rzeczpospolita [Oct 11] says politicians opened the public purse and Poland is now getting the bill, Business Insider Polska [Oct 11] reports economists floating new taxes as the government looks for money, INFOR [Oct 11] expects the March 2027 pension indexation to disappoint because of excessive debt, and Kuźmiuk of PiS argues every planned 2027 expense will have to be borrowed (wPolityce [Oct 11]). Money.pl [Oct 10] counters that the prudential threshold can be avoided without pain. On energy, Polskie Radio 24 [Oct 11] previews the EU summit on energy prices and asks what happens to Poland's reduced fuel VAT, and wholesale fuel prices stabilised over the weekend after a run of sharp increases (Super Biznes [Oct 11]). The NBP governance row persists after a Sejm commission recommended a State Tribunal vote on Glapiński (Bloomberg [Oct 9]).

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen's week was a study in contrasts: the stock led the WIG20 while former managers sat in custody over pre-election fuel pricing (TVN24 [Oct 8]), with wPolityce [Oct 11] recalling 2023 petrol sold at 5.99 zł; Orlen Neptun signed a training agreement for offshore wind in Świnoujście (GospodarkaMorska [Oct 11]). Dino's unions are threatening to halt trade just before the holidays (wGoleniowie, Kamienskie.info [Oct 11]), the first labour risk for a stock up 6.4% on the week. CD Projekt carries the Paramount Cyberpunk film (Reuters [Oct 9]) into the new week; KGHM has EU strategic-project status for two investments (StockWatch [Oct 9]). Housing: Kraków secondary prices are almost as high as Warsaw's (Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK [Oct 11]), Zero.pl [Oct 11] argues government attempts to lower prices do not work, and Business Insider Polska [Oct 11] explains the statutory mechanism for pausing mortgage instalments. Interia [Oct 11] canvasses scenarios for power price rises, and the government is preparing 4.8bn zł of energy support for industry (PulsHR [Oct 8]). In banks, Millennium's 154m zł of FX provisions (StockWatch [Oct 8]) and the Suwałki WIBOR ruling against PKO Bank Hipoteczny (CHF24 [Oct 8]) remain the overhang.

Geopolitics & Security: Police foiled an alleged plot to attack Prime Minister Tusk and the defence minister (NBC, Al Jazeera [Oct 11]). Poland told NATO to prepare for a deadly Russian hybrid attack (Financial Times [Oct 11]), NATO's commander said Ukraine aid will deter Putin's threat to Europe (Bloomberg [Oct 11]), and Poland and Norway are creating a NATO outpost in the Baltic (News.by [Oct 11]). The Warsaw Security Forum opened on Saturday (TVP World [Oct 10]), and Wąsik wants the eastern barrier built as fast as possible (wPolityce [Oct 11]).

New / Most Important: The assassination plot headlines add a domestic security premium to a week already defined by the NBP governance fight and a budget the opposition says must be entirely borrowed. None of it changes the rate path by itself, but the stack of institutional risk explains why the zloty cannot hold a rally despite 3.8% growth and a WIG near records.

Playbook ✓: Into the new week, stay with energy and retail leadership, keep banks underweight until the sovereign-crowding debate and WIBOR rulings clear, and use any dollar strength above 3.90 to add hedges rather than chase.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: BGK's call for EUR/PLN at 4.3 says the zloty is cheap on fundamentals; the market says fundamentals are not what is being traded, and the gap between the two is the opportunity only if the November projection restores a credible path.

Macro Stance: Indonesian government bonds are being shaken by high US yields, per Kompas.id reporting this week. The sovereign wealth fund's call for stock market transparency signals awareness that institutional capital is demanding governance reform before allocating.

New / Most Important: Indonesia is the canary in the EM coal mine for the 5%+ US yield regime — its deep domestic bond market makes it particularly vulnerable to foreign outflows when the US 10Y offers 5.24%.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None today — this is playing out exactly per the capital-flow playbook of strong dollar / high US yields pressuring EM local-currency debt.

Narrative: Mega-cap tech keeps carrying the market — the Nasdaq 100 at 30883 is ↑5.2% vs 4W against the Russell's ↓3.3%, a Russell/Nasdaq ratio down 8.1% — and AI-related companies are set to drive most third-quarter US earnings gains (Reuters, [Oct 9]).

Reported: TCS shares rose 4% as Q2 profit beat estimates and AI revenue crossed $3.1 Bn (BW Businessworld, [Oct 9]). Penguin Solutions' Q4 revenue jumped 68% and it raised FY27 guidance as AI infrastructure demand accelerates (TradingView, [Oct 6]). LG Electronics shares dropped as Q3 preliminary earnings missed estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 6]).

EPS Upside Watch: Snowflake — Wall Street is raising its price targets again (inkl, [Oct 8]), and JPMorgan favours it as the software rally extends (TradingView, [Oct 8]). Zscaler — eight firms raised price targets (24/7 Wall St., [Oct 7]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tech rallying into 5.24% yields is historically anomalous: mega-cap tech now trades as a cash-flow story, quasi-fixed-income with optionality. That holds only while earnings deliver, and OpenAI's $50 billion annualized revenue missed estimates, chilling AI optimism (bloomingbit, [Oct 9]) — any miss this season would expose the valuation stretch at once.

Narrative: The sector rides the mega-cap tailwind through META and GOOG on the same AI monetization narrative, and a sector outlook favours XLC and XLK on earnings leadership (Seeking Alpha, [Oct 9]).
Reported: Nihon Falcom significantly revised its yearly earnings forecast as its Kyoto Xanadu and Trails in the Sky remakes performed strongly (AUTOMATON, [Oct 7]).

EPS Upside Watch: Meta — Wells Fargo just put a $1,000 price target on the stock (24/7 Wall St., [Oct 7]). Alibaba — the stock rose over 4% as Bank of America says its "earnings inflection" is underpriced (TipRanks, [Oct 9]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.
Narrative: Big bank earnings begin this week as the first read on how 5%+ yields are reaching the real economy; the +44 bps 2s10s curve is a modest NIM tailwind, but credit quality is the wildcard.

Reported: Tryg shares rose 3% as its Q3 pre-tax profit beat consensus on benign claims (Investing.com, [Oct 9]). Bridgepoint raised its 2026 EBITDA guidance and introduced a new distribution policy (Yahoo Finance UK, [Oct 7]). IG Group fell again as Panmure cut its EBITDA forecast 18% after its profit warning (Share Talk, [Oct 5]).
EPS Upside Watch: Coinbase — Morgan Stanley raised its price target to $258 before earnings (CoinGape, [Oct 9]). Goldman Sachs — heads into earnings as dealmaking revives (Kalkine Media, [Oct 7]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Surging yields have already erased $270 billion in bank value into the earnings test (BigGo Finance, [Oct 10]). If banks now report wider loan-loss provisions alongside expanding NIMs, higher rates are lifting revenue while destroying asset quality — a mix that compresses P/Es despite earnings growth.

Narrative: WTI at 91.85 (↓8.2% vs 4W) is falling with the global manufacturing PMI at its highest since February 2022, so this is a supply story — China resuming October fuel exports after its holiday pause (Reuters, [Oct 9]) — not a demand-led selloff.
Reported: Shell expects its refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made (The Guardian, [Oct 7]). Spartan Delta lifted its guidance (Yahoo Finance Singapore, [Oct 8]).

EPS Upside Watch: US refiners — the industry enters earnings season with Goldman Sachs bullish on three Buy-rated companies (NAI500, [Oct 10]). European energy — European companies are set for 21% Q3 earnings growth, led by energy firms (The Economic Times, [Oct 9]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Oil falling 8% while equities make all-time highs is bullish for consumers and bearish for energy equity. If the Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" trending on X became policy, it would be a structural supply add that resets crude lower and could give the Fed room to pause — refiners' margins, not crude, would then carry the sector.
Narrative: Industrials are caught between strong fiscal spending pipelines and rising rates that compress multiples; ISM manufacturing still expanding at 54.5 is the positive demand signal.

Reported: Delta missed Q3 estimates and cut guidance on skyrocketing fuel costs (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 9]), though its CEO says demand is still strong (CNBC, [Oct 9]); the stock fell (Benzinga, [Oct 9]). Apogee raised fiscal 2027 guidance after second-quarter sales rose (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 6]). NORDEN raised its full-year guidance (Cyprus Shipping News, [Oct 9]).

EPS Upside Watch: PACCAR — earnings estimate upgrades might change the investment case (Simply Wall Street, [Oct 10]). Morgan Sindall — shares rose as the contractor expects results to beat forecasts (Kalkine Media, [Oct 9]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Record revenue did not save the quarter: Delta posted record revenue but cut its profit forecast (www.insideflyer.com, [Oct 9]) and warned of more airline capacity restraint as the fuel shock hits profits (Reuters, [Oct 9]). For airlines, capacity discipline, not demand, is now the bull case for fares.

Narrative: Retail sales data arrive this week; falling oil (↓8.2%) is a tailwind for consumer wallets, but 5%+ yields pressure credit-dependent spending, and the Russell's underperformance says the consumer-facing mid-cap cohort is struggling.

Reported: Aritzia surged the most in 18 months on earnings and a better outlook (Bloomberg.com, [Oct 9]) as revenue climbed 44% to $1.17 billion (Financial Post, [Oct 8]). Levi Strauss raised FY26 profit guidance but trimmed its sales growth outlook (TradingView, [Oct 7]), and slid on the guidance (Stocktwits, [Oct 8]). Uniqlo operator Fast Retailing posted a 32% rise in profit and beat forecasts (The Star, [Oct 8]).

EPS Upside Watch: Helen of Troy — UBS raised its price target to $29 on the earnings beat (Investing.com, [Oct 9]). Hasbro — UBS reiterated its Buy rating on Q3 beat expectations (Investing.com, [Oct 8]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retailers are getting smaller to earn more: from BJ's to Lululemon, they are trimming assortments to boost business (CNBC, [Oct 10]). With tariff refunds flattering this round of beats, as at Aritzia (Pluang, [Oct 9]), margin repair rather than volume is what the Mixed call is underwriting.
Narrative: Bond proxies suffer in a rising-yield environment: with the 10Y at 5.24% and climbing, staples' dividend yields are uncompetitive, and defensive money is going to mega-cap tech instead.

Reported: PepsiCo beat on international growth (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 8]) but cut its earnings forecast as the North American turnaround takes longer than expected (CNBC, [Oct 8]); the stock rallied (TIKR.com, [Oct 9]). Constellation Brands' Q2 topped estimates on beer and wine growth (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 7]), yet the stock slid on guidance and analyst cuts (Stocktwits, [Oct 8]). Tesco raised its 2026/27 profit guidance after H1 growth (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 9]).
EPS Upside Watch: Lamb Weston — beat on higher North America volume and lifted its full-year guidance (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 6]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The bear case is the yield, yet one bull argues PepsiCo's 4.6% yield at 15 times earnings still wins against a 5% Treasury (Seeking Alpha, [Oct 10]) — and the stock rallied on a guidance cut. Washed-out staples are trading on volume stability, not on the bond-proxy math.
Narrative: Another duration-sensitive sector under pressure from rising yields, though less so than staples given the growth optionality in biotech and medtech.

Reported: Neogen rose 8% on better-than-expected Q1 results and guidance (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 6]). AngioDynamics' Q1 beat estimates on Med Tech growth (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 9]), yet the stock slipped 4% (Yahoo Finance, [Oct 8]). Bavarian Nordic raised FY26 revenue guidance to DKK 6,100m on vaccine demand (scanx.trade, [Oct 7]).

EPS Upside Watch: Pfizer — four analysts raised their targets in one week without an upgrade (TIKR.com, [Oct 10]). AbbVie — HSBC raised its price target to $315 on immunology drug label expansions (NAI500, [Oct 7]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The optionality is in devices, not the defensives: analysts see medtech profit growth accelerating to 13% in Q1 next year, a two-year high (BigGo Finance, [Oct 10]). Q3 is the last weak quarter to buy into, which is why beats like AngioDynamics' are still being sold.

Narrative: Copper at 6.69 (↑3.4%) is the standout as the AI data-centre and power-grid metal, outperforming gold (↓4.4%), with demand support from a global manufacturing PMI at its highest since February 2022, boosted by AI spending.

Reported: Glencore raised its marketing profit guidance as Citi flags consensus upgrades (Proactive financial news, [Oct 5]). Caledonia Mining slid after cutting full-year production guidance and raising its cost outlook (Seeking Alpha, [Oct 9]). Wienerberger fell 4% as weak housing demand prompted a profit cut (Yahoo Finance UK, [Oct 6]).

EPS Upside Watch: Cascades — beat expectations and lifted its outlook (kalkine.ca, [Oct 9]). Lithium producers — Zimbabwe's lithium export earnings surge on higher spodumene prices (Mining.com, [Oct 7]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Industrial materials rallying while gold falls is an unusual cross-current — the two usually move together. The market is pricing a no-recession, higher-for-longer regime where industrial demand persists but safe-haven premiums compress, which is also why the gold miners are cutting output and the brickmakers are cutting profits.

Narrative: The worst sector to own at 5.24% on the 10Y — duration, leverage and cap rates all work against REITs — and Australian mortgage burdens at 1989 levels show what rising rates do to property.
